comments.author: @tjn0110
comments.text: Notice where the humans are hitting the ball, rarely does the ball land deeper than half-court, I find this rather odd and it seems intentional, it almost seems catering to the machine's (current) abilities, ie. while there are a couple deep shots in the video, does it have trouble with those?  The mechanism itself seems oddly placed deep into the court, when you are playing your paddle is often behind the court (as exhibited by the humans in both examples), only moving in on short balls, though we can't expect optimal machine paddle placement to be equal to optimal for human, just an observation.  The human around 4:05 is certainly hitting deeper into the court than the previous examples, and while we don't have a true side view, this machine, the paddle, appears to be positioned more towards the back of the court than the first, notice how it positions its paddle to the side, where the former machine tries to rest stretch centered, unhuman.

comments.author: @zxwxz
comments.text: I believe that VR will be an important infrastructure for robot training in the future. A highly realistic physics engine, along with creating digital twins of all robot-related components, will enable the construction of reinforcement learning in a virtual environment. This approach is definitely more likely to achieve goals than directly building robots. I think autonomous driving is also at a turning point from Alpha Go to Alpha Zero; the integrity of real-world data is no longer sufficient to cover all unexpected situations. In the future, countless virtual autonomous vehicles and corresponding sensing systems will be placed on virtual roads for environmental testing.
